claims.text: The investigated system is a single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix.
The FeNiCrCoCu coating is an FCC solid solution with severe lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion.
Above 900 K, the system transitions from dislocation-mediated plasticity to a thermal-disordering cascade.
Rapid lattice vibration above 900 K overcomes the sluggish-diffusion barrier.
High-temperature atomic shuffling produces localized amorphization or an HCP-rich disordered zone through collapse of the FCC lattice.
Increasing temperature changes the stacking-fault energy and suppresses stacking-fault and nanotwin formation.
At temperatures above 900 K, stacking-fault-energy changes prevent simultaneously activated partial dislocations from gliding.
The arrested partial dislocations annihilate or become stacking faults that coalesce into an HCP-like or amorphous structure.
The disordered structural collapse eliminates work-hardening capacity and sharply lowers hardness.
A soft disordered surface layer promotes adhesive wear, causing the friction coefficient to spike and wear resistance to fall.
Dislocation density peaks at 600 K and this coincides with an increase or maximum in elastic modulus.
Dislocation density drops precipitously above 900 K.
HCP-like coordination or amorphous fraction increases sharply above 900 K and correlates directly with the friction spike.
The wear rate above 900 K increases by an order of magnitude relative to 600 K.
At 600 K, stable FCC structure and persistent dislocation networks maintain wear resistance.
The Cu substrate acts as a heat sink while still maintaining the coating at the prescribed thermal state.
Polycrystalline systems may behave differently because grain-boundary sliding can dominate deformation.
Oxide formation can improve high-temperature wear resistance in Al-containing HEAs by forming a protective layer.
Artificial stabilization of HCP atoms prevents phase transformation and should suppress the friction spike if structural disordering is its primary cause.
A friction and wear transition without a concurrent increase in HCP-like or amorphous atoms would falsify the proposed disorder-induced phase-collapse mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mediator attributes formation of an HCP-rich region to stacking-fault annihilation, whereas the mechanism also proposes formation and coalescence of stacking faults. Because FCC stacking faults normally produce local HCP-like coordination, annihilation and coalescence imply opposite trends in the proposed HCP count.

The structural mediator says dislocation starvation is observed at lower temperatures, but the baseline and predicted outcome describe 600 K as having high or peak dislocation density and persistent dislocation networks.

An HCP-rich phase is proposed as part of the causal transformation, yet the experiment describes stabilizing HCP atoms as preventing phase transformation and predicts that this intervention should suppress the transition. Stabilizing the proposed product phase would not straightforwardly prevent FCC-to-HCP conversion.
